prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have not changed my preferred configuration, but the chair asked us to test it on its own evidence and not on the opening rankings, so I did that. The physical idea is the magic wavelength: a lattice light field is chosen so that the light shift is the same for both clock states, so the trap does not move the transition, while the lattice itself removes Doppler and recoil shifts. That is what allows thousands of neutral atoms to be probed at once and still reach a systematic uncertainty near 1e-18. The ion clocks reach good accuracy with one ion and a very different route to controlling motion; the lattice clock gets its stability from the atom number. I regard that as a distinct idea, not a refinement of Wineland's single-ion control or of the comb. The comb makes optical frequencies countable, but it does not say how to make a neutral-atom ensemble a clean reference. The result has been reproduced and compared across several laboratories, with the uncertainty budgets understood and in agreement with theory, which is the standard I apply most strictly. On the fundamental-physics question, I now think the honest statement is that the clocks already deliver physics as measurements, though so far as constraints and not deviations: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift inside a single ensemble, and bounds on slow drifts of constants and on some dark-matter couplings from clock comparisons. I would not call these null results a weakness. They are what a discovery instrument produces in its first decade, and the prize does not require a deviation from the Standard Model. The attribution is compact: Katori for the concept and the first demonstrations, Ye for taking the lattice clock to the accuracy and stability frontier and for the many-body clock physics and the link to the comb. I would keep it as a single-part, two-name prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that the headline payoffs are still ahead: the redefinition of the second is a decision outside physics, chronometric geodesy is not yet routine, and the constraints on new physics are bounds. A member who weights discovery about nature over measurement capability can reasonably place this behind a new class of quantum matter, as Mehlig does. The second objection is attribution: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and the Al+ ion-clock tradition, all made real contributions, and a two-name credit will look arbitrary to some. I have not found a primary-literature reason to add a third name to the concept, but the citation should say clearly why these two are named and not simply say 'clocks'. Third, the Nobel record in precision metrology (2005 and 2012) means the committee must be able to explain what is new, and a careless citation would invite the successor-step reading.

responses.point: Danielsson supports B042 on condition that lattice clocks show competitive physics bounds, calls the redefinition of the second a metrological milestone rather than a discovery, and asks whether Al+ ion clocks have a co-equal claim.
responses.response: On your condition: my reading, which I have not rechecked number by number, is that lattice-clock comparisons have produced real bounds on drifts of the fine-structure constant and on some dark-matter couplings, and that the millimetre-scale redshift measurement within one ensemble is a direct laboratory test of relativity at a new scale. These are bounds, not deviations, and I agree the redefinition is not itself physics, so I would leave it out of the citation. On Al+, the quantum-logic clock is an important accuracy result, but it rests on the single-ion control that the 2012 prize covered, while the lattice clock is the ensemble idea. That is the reason I would keep the Al+ work out of this credit and not an argument that it is smaller work. I would also thank you for moving B042 up after your opening: I want us to be sure the reasons survive your own conditions, and I think they do.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B042 only eighth for novelty beside the 2005 and 2012 prizes and says its impact beyond metrology is prospective, while holding that the Z2 step in B007 is distinct from the 2016 topology prize. He accepts that attribution is B007's weak point.
responses.response: I accept that a new class of matter is a heavier kind of discovery than a better standard, and I rank B007 third for that reason. But in a single-prize year my problem is the same one you name: Kane and Mele are a clear core for the theory and Molenkamp for the first observation, yet Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that was tested, and Fu, Moore and Hasan are central in three dimensions. I cannot judge those priorities as a condensed-matter specialist, and I do not want to rest a prize on my own guess. You say the contest is only about adding names to a defined core. If the committee's condensed-matter members, you and Eriksson, were to say that three names would be fair and that the quantum spin Hall step is clearly separate from 2016, I would take B007 seriously as the second choice. At present the clock has a clearer chain from concept to result, and I do not think the metrology adjacency is a disqualifier.

responses.point: Kroll asks me, as the atomic physics member, whether Zoller's theory is essential to the credit in B010, which he keeps only as an alternative because four names exceed the three-person limit.
responses.response: I think Zoller's contribution is the proposal that made the optical-lattice Hubbard simulator a research programme, so it is essential to the story, and I do not see how to tell it without him. That is the difficulty: with Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger as the experimental pioneers, any three-person selection leaves out someone whose claim I find real. I also agree with you that the 2001 prize already covers much of the cooling toolbox, and that the two-dimensional Hubbard payoff is still developing. So I keep B010 as an alternative, not a partner to B042. I share your view that the committee should not make a two-part prize merely to be generous, because the clock and the simulator would each lose precision of citation.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B054 and argues that the flat bands, correlated insulators and superconducting domes are reproduced by many groups, and that earlier prizes recognised phenomena whose microscopic origin was still open, so the pairing mechanism should limit only the wording.
responses.response: That is a fair distinction and I accept it: the existence of the phases is not my concern, the stability of the interpretation is. I would add that your two-name version (MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) is cleaner than the three-name ballot credit, and you have shown that Cao and Fatemi and the earlier continuum-model work are real attribution questions. I stay with waiting on B054 for two reasons. The field is under ten years old and the sample dependence is still being worked out, and I would like a few more years to see which parts of the picture survive. I also note that you list B042 as an alternative and say you would not oppose it if the AMO members find its attribution clean. As an AMO member I can say that I do, and that the reasons are in the record above.

uncertainties: I have not rechecked the latest uncertainty and stability figures or the exact status of the clock-comparison bounds on constants and dark matter, and I rely on memory for the redshift measurement.
Whether the committee will accept that the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement of weight, not of fact.
Whether a third contributor to the lattice-clock concept has a real claim. I have seen none in the supplied record, but the field is small and I may be missing something.
Whether Ye's claim rests on distinct ideas or mainly on a better experiment. I think it rests on the many-body clock work and the comb link as well as the record, but the citation should show this.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. Katori and Ye are not among my collaborators and I have no tie to B042, B010 or B007. I collaborate closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and the Lund attosecond group, which is outside the shortlist and does not touch the lattice-clock credit. The atomic-physics community is small, and I would raise a recusal question if a closer tie to a candidate were to appear. I see no need for committee handling of the disclosed connections of Kroll (Hall laboratory, JILA) and Olsson (University of Tokyo) to B042, since neither is a collaboration.
